directed-fix-finding-schema.headline: The "valid but out-of-scope" disposition could never actually be assigned
directed-fix-finding-schema.what: The finding schema defines a disposition called `triaged-out` for findings that are real but belong to a different story (e.g. spun into a backlog stub). But the schema's own processing rules made that outcome unreachable: Rule 1 sent every legitimate routine finding to `fixed`, Rule 2 sent every legitimate stakes-class finding to `escalated`, and the only rule that could produce `triaged-out` fired exclusively when the finding was NOT legitimate. So a legitimate-but-out-of-scope finding had no path to the disposition that was built for it.
directed-fix-finding-schema.why_it_matters: A reviewer could never correctly route a valid finding that belongs to a different component or is tracked separately — it would be forced into `fixed` (auto-fixing work that doesn't belong to this story) or `escalated`, instead of being triaged out to the backlog. The schema's processing rules directly contradict its own field definition and the governing spec §4 contract, and it violates AC 14 (disposition rules must be internally self-consistent).
directed-fix-finding-schema.evidence: Line 70: '`triaged-out` | The finding is valid but out of scope for this story...'  Line 105 (Rule 3): 'When `legitimate` is `false`, the fixer sets `disposition` to `dismissed` (with a non-empty rationale) or `triaged-out`.'  Spec line 178-179: '...or emits a triage stub for genuinely out-of-scope new work.'  Spec line 296: '`triaged-out` | New out-of-scope work; spun into a backlog stub via momentum:triage'.
directed-fix-finding-schema.resolution: Fixed: Added Rule 4 covering legitimate-but-out-of-scope findings, which sets disposition to `triaged-out` and spins a backlog stub via momentum:triage. Rule 3 was narrowed to dismissed-only for non-legitimate findings, explicitly excluding triaged-out from that path. The triaged-out disposition is now reachable for legitimate out-of-scope work, matching the line 70 definition and the spec §4 contract (fix commit 25ffb4d).

directed-fix-finding-schema.why_it_matters: Because this doc is the canonical contract two artifacts must agree on, a reviewer that emits `verdict: PASS`, `severity: blocker`, or `source: bmad-code-review` per the spec would not match the doc's stated examples — a drift risk for interoperability. The omitted source list understates who feeds the schema, hiding architecture-guard, e2e-validator, and simplify as contributors. (Note: the fields are typed as open strings, so this was not a hard schema break or an AC violation — hence low severity.)

directed-fix-finding-schema.resolution: Fixed: Reconciled all three fields in both the Base Fields table and the Full Finding Shape YAML block — source now lists bmad-code-review|avfl|qa-reviewer|architecture-guard|e2e-validator|simplify, verdict shows PASS|FAIL|BLOCKED, and severity shows blocker|critical|major|minor|low. conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.headline: The per-story merge loop told the Conductor to stop and ask the developer on conflicts — the spec says it must never stop
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.what: The Conductor is the sole authority for git mutations and is required by the spec to resolve merge conflicts autonomously (resolve itself or fire a dev subagent, then retry) and to NEVER halt for the developer during the git lifecycle. But the per-story merge loop in the scaffold instead instructed `If rebase conflicts: HALT for developer resolution`. This was in the live merge loop, not inside the explicitly hollow/deferred placeholder blocks, so it actively asserted the wrong behavior.
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.why_it_matters: A routine rebase conflict during the build would stop the whole run and interrupt the developer — a touchpoint AC 7 says must not exist on the routine path (only run-start and end-gate). Because the conflict-resolution engine is owned by a downstream story (conduct-merge-and-conflict-resolution), baking a developer HALT into the scaffold pre-commits the wrong default that downstream work would have to unwind.
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.evidence: workflow.md:129 `- If rebase conflicts: HALT for developer resolution.` vs spec line 21/116/424 ("Never HALT" / "Zero developer HALT exists anywhere in the git lifecycle"); conflict resolution is delegated to story conduct-merge-and-conflict-resolution (stories/index.json).
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.resolution: Fixed: Replaced `If rebase conflicts: HALT for developer resolution` with an autonomous resolution placeholder — the Conductor resolves conflicts or fires a fixer subagent, then retries, never halting (per spec decision #9; conflict-resolution engine deferred to the conduct-merge-and-conflict-resolution story). The placeholder points at the correct invariant without pre-committing implementation details (fix commit d1d41a0).

conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.headline: The final sprint-to-main merge also told the Conductor to halt on conflicts instead of resolving them
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.what: In the end-gate approve sequence, the scaffold merges the sprint branch into main and instructed `If conflicts: HALT for developer resolution`. The spec specifies this final merge the same way as all other merges — the Conductor resolves conflicts and retries — under the same never-halt git policy.
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.why_it_matters: It hardcodes a behavior the spec assigns to autonomous Conductor conflict resolution, pre-committing the wrong default for the final merge. (This HALT sits past the human end-gate, so it does not add a routine pre-acceptance touchpoint and does not violate AC 11 — which is why it is lower severity than the per-story case.)
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.evidence: workflow.md:308 `3. If conflicts: HALT for developer resolution.` vs spec line 72 ("merge sprint branch → main (Conductor resolves conflicts; retry)").
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.resolution: Fixed: Replaced `If conflicts: HALT for developer resolution` with an autonomous resolution placeholder citing spec §2 and decision #9, consistent with the per-story fix; the fixer-subagent delegation is noted as delivered by the downstream conflict-resolution story (fix commit d1d41a0).

conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.headline: The workflow's list of developer touchpoints left out the push confirmation that the spec counts as one of the two
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.what: The workflow header enumerates exactly two routine developer touchpoints — run start and end-gate (plus the narrow escalation exception) — matching AC 7's wording. But the spec counts its two routine touchpoints differently: the end-gate conversation and the push confirmation (folded into approve), treating run-start as a pre-flight guard rather than a routine touchpoint. The spine includes a real `<ask>Push to origin/main?` on the routine path that its own touchpoint summary did not list.
conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.why_it_matters: A definitional mismatch, not a behavioral bug: the push-ask is mandated by git-discipline and is explicitly folded into the approve sequence by the spec, so it sits inside the end-gate and does not constitute a second mandatory acceptance gate (AC 11 still holds). But the touchpoint accounting reads inconsistently with the spec until clarified.

conduct-skill-scaffold-and-spine.resolution: Fixed: Added a clarifying parenthetical to the Touchpoint 2 entry stating that the push confirmation is folded into the end-gate/approve sequence per spec §2 line 76 and git-discipline, not a separate acceptance gate. This aligns the spine's accounting with the spec without changing any behavior (fix commit d1d41a0).

code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.headline: Code-reviewer skill only suggests reading its workflow instead of ordering the agent to follow it
code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.what: The code-reviewer SKILL.md ends with a passive pointer — 'See workflow.md for the full execution protocol' — rather than the imperative 'load and follow' dispatch that every other Momentum skill uses to make its workflow binding. The non-interactive/report-only guarantee depends on the workflow actually being executed.

code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.resolution: Fixed: replaced 'See `workflow.md` for the full execution protocol.' with the imperative dispatch 'Load and follow `./workflow.md` — it is the binding execution protocol for every adapter run.', consistent with every other Momentum skill. Re-check returned CLEAN.

code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.headline: Skill claims it passes triage buckets through 'unchanged' but it actually overrides the engine's drop-dismiss behavior
code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.what: SKILL.md says the adapter 'passes through the engine's internal triage buckets unchanged,' but workflow.md step 4 deliberately overrides the underlying engine's 'Drop all dismiss findings' instruction and retains them instead. The bucket labels are unchanged, but the engine's drop action is changed — making the word 'unchanged' look self-contradictory.
code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.why_it_matters: The override is the correct behavior for AC4 (return findings in full, do not swallow). The defect is purely descriptive: a reader reconciling the SKILL.md summary against the engine's actual triage step could conclude the adapter contradicts itself or misdescribes its own behavior. No behavioral bug — a wording-precision issue.

code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.resolution: Fixed: rewrote the description to 'It preserves the engine's triage bucket labels (patch / defer / dismiss / decision_needed) but, unlike the standalone engine, retains dismiss findings rather than dropping them — so the Conductor receives the full set.' This distinguishes label preservation from the intentional drop-action override. Re-check returned CLEAN.

code-review-adapter-noninteractive-drive.what: The actionable error template the adapter emits when _bmad/bmm/config.yaml is missing embeds HTML-escaped angle brackets (<your-project-name>, <your-name>) inside its operator-facing output block. This is the only operator-facing string the story produces, and AC6 requires a clear, actionable error — a literal entity in a copy-pasteable scaffold is a papercut against that. dev-read-contract-part-a-header.headline: Contract-file discovery leaves the file extension as a guess across five possibilities with no lookup step

conduct-preflight-halts.headline: The H4 stalled-state guard prints an unbound placeholder instead of naming which stories are blocked

conduct-build-phase-frontier.headline: The build emits a status-transition to 'blocked' — a state the tool does not recognize, so the command errors
conduct-build-phase-frontier.what: When a story exhausts its retries, the frontier issues `status-transition --target blocked (or nearest available state)`. But 'blocked' is in neither the tool's ORDERED_STATES nor TERMINAL_STATES, so the validator returns 'Unknown target state: blocked' and the transition fails. There is no 'blocked' story state — it is purely Conductor in-memory state.
conduct-build-phase-frontier.why_it_matters: The command as written fails at runtime, so a story that genuinely cannot complete is never given a valid durable status — the build can't record the outcome correctly. The correct durable state is 'dropped' or 'closed-incomplete' (both valid from a non-terminal state).

conduct-build-phase-frontier.resolution: Fixed: replaced `--target blocked` with `--target closed-incomplete` at the exhausted-retries branch, added an inline note clarifying that 'blocked' is Conductor in-memory state ({{blocked}} array) only with 'dropped' as the valid alternative, and updated the end-of-build completion sweep to use `--target closed-incomplete` for stranded dependents. Re-check returned REFIXED (story had a separate residual).

But the schema reserves 'fixed' for routine class and 'escalated' for stakes-class findings raised to the human. Any finding that reached the mid-flight pause is by definition stakes-class and was raised, so its disposition must be 'escalated.'

The Halt and Dismiss branches use the correct terms; only Continue is wrong.

Stakes class only'. conduct-stakes-timing-escalation-mechanism.md L60 AC9. workflow.md L311-312 records disposition: "fixed" for a stakes-class mid-flight finding. conduct-build-phase-frontier.headline: A build-invalidating finding arriving via the 'failed' signal silently bypasses the mid-flight escalation hook

But the narrow mid-flight bar explicitly includes 'build-invalidating' findings — exactly the kind that would prevent a story from reaching 'merged' and surface as 'failed' instead, which never reaches the hook.

conduct-build-phase-frontier.headline: A story stranded at 'in-progress' by a crashed prior run is silently abandoned

The diff models 'blocked' as a Conductor-internal categorization rather than a pipeline-emitted signal, which is defensible, but it diverges from the explicit three-signal enumeration without acknowledging the reconciliation.

Reconciles the two-signal model with spec §3's three-term list. Re-check returned REFIXED.

conduct-build-phase-frontier.headline: RESIDUAL: The crash-recovery reset command omits --force, so the backward status transition is rejected at runtime

Use --force to override"`

code-review-adapter-repoint-sprint-dev.headline: Per-story code review diffs the wrong commit range, so most stories get the wrong code reviewed

Because all stories merge sequentially onto one sprint branch before review runs, that tip-relative offset only lands on the right boundary for the single last-merged story. Every earlier story gets a truncated, empty, or polluted diff.
code-review-adapter-repoint-sprint-dev.why_it_matters: The code-review adapter trusts whatever diff it is handed and does not scan git state to find its own target ('the diff is the input, full stop'). A wrong diff means the wrong code gets reviewed with no self-correction — real changes in earlier-merged stories escape review entirely. This breaks AC3 (per-story review must match what the adapter emits on that story's true diff) and undermines AC4's promise that 'what it reviews' is preserved.

Compare line 369 which correctly says 'identify the commit before the first sprint merge / find the merge boundary' rather than tip-relative `~N`.

Note: re-check found this fix introduced a new residual bug (the three-dot form is empty under sprint-dev's fast-forward merges) — see the residual card below; that was subsequently fixed in commit 9add6b7.

But `sprint/{sprint}~N` is a pure ancestry offset that counts every commit on the branch — including other stories' commits and merge commits — regardless of which files they touched. The two numbers only agree in a degenerate single-story case.
